The dwarf round herring Jenkinsia lamprotaenia is a small, schooling clupeiform fish widely distributed across the tropical western Atlantic. Individuals of this species attain a modest maximum size, with the ultimate total length reaching 7.5 cm [Li = 7.5 cm] in the sampled populations off the Caribbean coast. Under the prevailing warm-water conditions of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], the embryonic development proceeds quite rapidly, and the age at birth or larval eclosion occurs after just 6 days [ab = 6 days]. This abbreviated incubation period is characteristic of many small, pelagic-spawning clupeids and is presumably an adaptation to high predation pressure on the vulnerable egg stage. The dry weight at birth, derived from the diameter of the yolk-laden eggs, is minute, calculated at approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams] at 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C]. Such a small initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the endotrophic larva before it must initiate first exogenous feeding, a critical transitional phase in its early life history.

At the same stable thermal regime of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], the onset of sexual maturation occurs at a total length of approximately 2.8 cm [Lp = approximately 2.8 cm], a size at which individuals attain puberty. Reaching this developmental milestone is directly linked to body size rather than chronological age, as is common among small pelagic fishes. The wet weight at this pubertal transition is estimated to be around 0.1985 grams [Wwp = around 0.1985 grams], a value derived from length–weight relationships established for the species. This weight represents a substantial increase over the neonatal mass, reflecting the rapid somatic growth achieved during the larval and juvenile phases. Achieving sexual maturity at this relatively small size suggests a life-history strategy oriented toward early reproduction, which may be advantageous in environments characterized by high adult mortality.

At the typical habitat temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%] during the spawning season. This value is consistent with that of other small, iteroparous clupeiforms that produce multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended breeding period. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult has been calculated as 4.9 grams [Wwi = 4.9 grams], reached when the fish approaches its asymptotic length. This adult mass represents the culmination of the rapid growth phase that slows considerably after sexual maturation. In comparison to the mass at puberty, the increase from 0.1985 grams to 4.9 grams highlights a significant post-pubertal growth trajectory that continues well after the fish has become reproductively active.

Longevity in this species is constrained by its small body size and high metabolic demands in a warm-water environment. The maximum lifespan has been documented to reach approximately 1095 days [am = approximately 1095 days] under field conditions at a water temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C], equivalent to about three years. This relatively short life expectancy is typical of small pelagic fishes that exhibit rapid maturation and high natural mortality rates. A three-year lifespan, equivalent to approximately 36 months, places the dwarf round herring among the shorter-lived members of the Clupeidae family. Throughout this relatively brief existence, individuals undergo a remarkable transformation from a tiny, yolk-dependent larva weighing just half a milligram to a reproductively active adult of several grams. The interplay between this abbreviated lifespan and the early age at puberty underscores a life-history strategy optimized for rapid turnover and high reproductive output within a narrow demographic window.

From a broader ecological perspective, the life-history traits of Jenkinsia lamprotaenia position it as a quintessential r-selected species within its pelagic habitat. The small ultimate total length of 7.5 cm [Li = 7.5 cm] allows it to exploit zooplanktonic prey resources that are inaccessible to larger predators, while its schooling behavior mitigates predation risk. The rapid developmental rate, culminating in eclosion after just 6 days [ab = 6 days] at 26.8 °C, enables multiple spawning events within a single breeding season, and the gonadosomatic index was 4% [GSI = 4%] at a temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C] at a temperature of 26.8 °C [T = 26.8 °C]. These traits collectively facilitate the persistence of stable populations despite the intense mortality pressures typical of tropical epipelagic ecosystems. Comparisons with other small clupeids, such as the anchovy Engraulis encrasicolus, reveal a convergent set of life-history solutions to similar ecological challenges, albeit with species-specific calibrations in the timing and magnitude of each life-history transition.
